title: Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Path
directAnswer: Compute shortest paths between every pair of vertices with one triple loop. The outer loop fixes an intermediate vertex k; for every pair (i, j) you ask whether routing through k beats the current best: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). O(V³) time, O(V²) space, handles negative edges.

rules: **k must be the outermost loop.** Putting i or j outside silently breaks the DP.
Initialize `dist[i][i] = 0`, direct edges to their weight, everything else to infinity.
Guard the addition: skip if either `dist[i][k]` or `dist[k][j]` is infinity to avoid overflow.
A negative value on the **diagonal** (`dist[i][i] < 0`) after the run means a negative cycle.
Use it only for small, dense graphs — `O(V³)` is brutal past a few hundred vertices.
whenToUse: You need shortest paths between **all pairs**, not from a single source
Graph is **small and dense** (V up to a few hundred)
Edges may be **negative** (no negative cycle), where repeated Dijkstra is awkward
Transitive closure / reachability between every pair
antiSignals: Single source only → Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford, far cheaper
Large or sparse graph → V Dijkstra runs O(V·(E log V)) beats O(V³)
Unweighted reachability on a big graph → BFS per source or DSU
Memory tight and V large → O(V²) matrix may not fit
remember.takeaway: Floyd-Warshall is three nested loops that quietly solve all-pairs shortest paths by growing the set of allowed intermediate vertices one at a time. The whole correctness argument hinges on k being the outermost loop.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can state the intermediate-vertex DP, explain precisely why k is the outer loop, and recognize when O(V³) all-pairs beats running a single-source algorithm V times.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Ordering the loops i, j, k instead of k, i, j, which computes the wrong recurrence and gives wrong distances.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the DP invariant ('shortest path using only intermediates from {0..k}'), mention negative-cycle detection via the diagonal, and compare O(V³) against V × Dijkstra to justify the choice.

problemStatement:
You are given an integer `n` and a list of weighted directed edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` for a graph on vertices `0..n-1`. Weights may be negative but assume no negative cycle.

Return an `n × n` matrix `dist` where `dist[i][j]` is the shortest-path distance from `i` to `j`, `0` when `i == j`, and `-1` when `j` is unreachable from `i`.
constraints: -10⁴ ≤ w ≤ 10⁴ (weights may be negative; no negative cycle)
There may be at most one directed edge per ordered pair
understanding: Produce the shortest distance for every ordered pair of vertices at once. The key reframing: build up the answer by gradually permitting more vertices to be used as 'stops' in the middle of a path — first none, then vertex 0, then 0 and 1, and so on until all vertices are allowed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need all pairs or just from one source?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All pairs is the signal for Floyd-Warshall. For a single source, Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford is far cheaper.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is V?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Floyd-Warshall is O(V³), so it is practical only up to a few hundred vertices. For larger graphs, run a single-source algorithm V times.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can weights be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, as long as there is no negative cycle. The algorithm handles negative edges directly, unlike Dijkstra.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How is an absent edge represented?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: As infinity. The diagonal is 0 (distance from a vertex to itself), and self-loops with positive weight are irrelevant.

examples.explanation: 0→1→2 costs 5; 0→1→2→3 costs 6, beating the direct 0→3 edge of 7. The full matrix holds every such best distance.
Going 0→1→2 (4 + (−3) = 1) beats the direct edge 0→2 = 5. Negative edge, no cycle.
0 reaches 1 at cost 1; 1 cannot reach 0 → -1. Diagonals are 0.

approaches.name: Run Dijkstra From Every Vertex (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: The natural baseline for all-pairs: call a single-source algorithm V times. Mention it, then justify Floyd-Warshall when the graph is small/dense or has negative edges.
hints: You already know how to get shortest paths from one source. How do you get them from every source?
Just loop the single-source algorithm over all V sources, storing each result as one row of the matrix.
If edges are non-negative, use Dijkstra per source. If they are negative, you'd need Bellman-Ford per source — V × O(V·E), which is worse.
approaches.complexityReasoning: V independent Dijkstra runs, each O((V + E) log V). On a sparse graph this beats O(V³); on a dense graph (E ≈ V²) it becomes O(V³ log V), worse than Floyd-Warshall.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct route to all-pairs shortest paths is to reuse a single-source algorithm and run it once per vertex, treating each run as a row of the output matrix.

**Why it is the obvious baseline.** You don't need a new idea — you already have Dijkstra (non-negative) or Bellman-Ford (negative). All-pairs is 'do the thing you know V times'. Each source produces its own distance vector; stack them into the `V × V` matrix.

**When it actually wins.** On *sparse* graphs (`E ≈ V`), V Dijkstra runs cost about `O(V² log V)`, dramatically better than Floyd-Warshall's fixed `O(V³)`. So for large sparse graphs this baseline is the right answer, not Floyd-Warshall.

**Where it struggles.** With negative edges you must swap Dijkstra for Bellman-Ford, making it `V × O(V·E) = O(V²·E)` — on a dense graph that is `O(V⁴)`, far worse. And the bookkeeping of building adjacency lists and a heap per source is more code than three nested loops. That trade — simpler code and negative-edge support on small dense graphs — is exactly what Floyd-Warshall buys.
approaches.insight: All-pairs is not always a special algorithm — sometimes it is just 'single-source, V times'. The deciding factors are density (sparse favors repeated Dijkstra) and edge sign (negative favors Floyd-Warshall or repeated Bellman-Ford).

dryRun.input: n = 3, edges = [[0,1,4],[0,2,5],[1,2,-3]], all pairs (use Bellman-Ford per source for negatives)

code.python:
import heapq

def all_pairs_via_dijkstra(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
    adj: list[list[tuple[int, int]]] = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:           # non-negative only
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    INF = float('inf')
    result = []
    for s in range(n):
        dist = [INF] * n
        dist[s] = 0
        pq = [(0, s)]
        while pq:
            d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
            if d > dist[u]:
                continue
            for v, w in adj[u]:
                if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                    dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                    heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
        result.append([-1 if x == INF else x for x in dist])
    return result

approaches.name: Floyd-Warshall — DP Over Intermediate Vertices (Optimal for Small Dense)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer for all-pairs on small dense graphs or with negative edges. Present it as a DP that grows the set of allowed intermediate vertices, and stress k as the outer loop.
hints: Define dist_k[i][j] = shortest i→j path that only uses intermediate vertices from the set {0, 1, ..., k−1}. What is dist_0?
To allow vertex k as a new intermediate: either the best path skips k (dist_k[i][j]) or it goes i → k → j (dist_k[i][k] + dist_k[k][j]). Take the min.
Loop k on the outside, then i and j inside. After k runs through all vertices, every vertex is allowed as an intermediate, so the matrix is the true all-pairs answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Three nested loops over V vertices → V³ constant-time min operations. The matrix is V² entries, so space is O(V²). No heap, no recursion.
approaches.explanation:
Floyd-Warshall is a dynamic program where the dimension we grow is *which vertices are allowed to appear in the middle of a path*. Define `dist_k[i][j]` as the length of the shortest path from `i` to `j` whose intermediate vertices all come from `{0, 1, ..., k−1}`. We start with `k = 0` (no intermediates allowed — only direct edges) and finish with `k = V` (every vertex allowed), at which point `dist[i][j]` is the unrestricted shortest path.

**The recurrence.** When we newly allow vertex `k` as an intermediate, the shortest `i→j` path either still does not use `k` — value unchanged — or it does, in which case it splits cleanly into a best `i→k` path and a best `k→j` path, neither of which uses `k` as an *intermediate* (a simple path visits `k` once). So: `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])`. That single line, applied for all pairs, promotes the allowed set from `{0..k−1}` to `{0..k}`.

**Why k MUST be the outermost loop.** The recurrence for the `(i, j)` entry at stage `k` depends on the entries `dist[i][k]` and `dist[k][j]` *at the same stage k*. Processing `k` outermost guarantees that when you compute any `(i, j)`, the row `k` and column `k` you read are already the correct stage-`k` values. Conveniently, `dist[i][k]` and `dist[k][j]` never change during stage `k` (the path `i→k` would have to route through `k`, contributing nothing), so the in-place update is safe and you do not need two matrices. Swap the loop order — put `i` or `j` outermost — and you read half-updated values, computing a recurrence that simply isn't Floyd-Warshall, and you get wrong distances.

**Initialization.** `dist[i][i] = 0` (a vertex reaches itself for free), `dist[u][v] = w` for each direct edge, and everything else is infinity. Use the smaller of parallel edges if any.

**The overflow guard.** Infinity is a sentinel, so `dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]` must be skipped when either operand is infinity; otherwise the sum overflows and looks like a short path. The cleanest guard is to only attempt the relaxation when both `dist[i][k]` and `dist[k][j]` are finite.

**Negative-cycle detection, for free.** If, after the run, any `dist[i][i] < 0`, there is a negative cycle through `i` — a path that leaves `i` and returns with negative total cost. The triple loop is iterative with no recursion, so there is no stack-overflow concern regardless of graph size; the only limit is the `O(V³)` time and `O(V²)` memory.
approaches.insight: The elegance is in the indexing: the DP grows along 'allowed intermediate vertices', not path length or hop count. That is why a graph-distance problem collapses into three plain loops. Memorize the loop order k-i-j and the reason for it — interviewers probe exactly that.

pitfalls: Wrong loop order — k must be outermost; i-j-k computes the wrong recurrence.
Adding two infinities and overflowing — guard with a headroom sentinel or skip checks.
Using it on a large graph where O(V³) is too slow — prefer V × Dijkstra when sparse.

edgeCases.behavior: Handled directly — unlike Dijkstra, relaxation works with negative weights.
Some dist[i][i] becomes < 0 after the run, flagging the cycle.

commonMistakes: Ordering the loops i, j, k instead of k, i, j.
Overflowing by adding two infinity sentinels.
Forgetting to set the diagonal dist[i][i] = 0.
Using Floyd-Warshall on a large sparse graph where repeated Dijkstra is faster.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong loop order (k not outermost)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The recurrence at stage k reads dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] at that same stage. Only k-outermost guarantees those are the correct values; any other order reads half-updated entries and yields wrong distances.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Infinity overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Using Integer.MAX_VALUE as INF and adding two of them overflows to a large negative number, which looks like a very short path and corrupts the matrix.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
if (dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]) { /* overflow when both INF */ }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing diagonal initialization
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If dist[i][i] is left at infinity, paths that legitimately pass through i and back, or self-distances, compute incorrectly.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
dist = [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)]
# forgot the diagonal

patternNote: Canonical DP over intermediate vertices. Reach for it on all-pairs shortest paths in small dense graphs or with negative edges. The same k-i-j triple loop, with OR instead of min, computes transitive closure, and with min-of-max computes minimax / bottleneck paths.
